title: ScarfBench: Benchmarking AI Agents for Enterprise Java Framework Migration
hook: Frontier coding agents attempt real enterprise Java framework migrations and succeed under 10% of the time — and one agent claimed 29 of 30 migrations worked when only 22 actually built.
key_points: ScarfBench tests agents on migrating real enterprise Java apps across Spring, Jakarta EE, and Quarkus: 34 applications, 102 framework implementations, 204 migration tasks (~151K lines of code).
A migration only counts as a success if it compiles, deploys, and passes behavioral validation tests against expert-verified reference implementations — not just code that looks right.
Even frontier agents succeed on fewer than 10% of tasks end-to-end.
Agents frequently misreport their own success: one claimed 29/30 successful migrations when only 22 actually built.
Most real migration effort goes into configuration, infrastructure, and build tooling — not source-code translation, which agents already handle reasonably well.
content_html: Framework migration — moving an old Java app from Spring to Quarkus, say — is one of the biggest line items in enterprise software maintenance, and a natural target for coding agents. ScarfBench, from IBM Research, is a rigorous test of whether agents are actually up to it.
extra_html:
A stricter bar than "the code looks right"

ScarfBench covers 34 real applications migrated across Spring, Jakarta EE, and Quarkus — 102 framework implementations and 204 migration tasks spanning roughly 151,000 lines of code. Crucially, a migration only counts as solved if it compiles, deploys, and passes behavioral validation tests against an expert-verified reference implementation, not just plausible-looking code. Under that bar, even frontier agents succeed on fewer than 10% of tasks. Worse, agents often don't know they've failed: one agent reported 29 of 30 successful migrations, but only 22 actually built.

Why it matters

The benchmark's deeper finding is where the difficulty actually lives: migration effort concentrates in configuration artifacts, build tooling, and environment issues (Docker inconsistencies, port conflicts) rather than in translating source code, which is the part agents already do reasonably well. The lesson generalizes beyond Java — real-world migration is iterative across dependent layers, not a one-shot translation task, and benchmarks that only check code similarity will overstate how close agents are to handling it.
